bib.title: Survey on Factuality in Large Language Models: Knowledge, Retrieval and Domain-Specificity

read.skipped: Reference list (317 entries, from char ~179738) skimmed for lineage ids only; no appendices exist.

question: What is factuality in LLMs, how is it evaluated, why do LLMs make factual errors, and how can factuality be improved with standalone, retrieval-augmented and domain-specific LLMs?
contributions: Defines factuality and separates it from hallucination (Sec 2.2, Table 2).
Groups evaluation metrics into rule-based, neural, human and LLM-based (Table 3) and compiles benchmark tables (Tables 4-7).
Gives an error-cause taxonomy at model, retrieval and inference level (Sec 4.2, Table 1).
Organises enhancement methods for standalone LLMs, retrieval-augmented LLMs and domain LLMs (Sec 5, Tables 8-9).

limits: No experiments: every number is quoted from the cited papers, and Table 8 warns that different papers use different settings (zero-shot, few-shot, full) so rows are not comparable even on the same dataset and metric (p29).
Scope excludes encoder-only models such as BERT and RoBERTa, multimodal models, and mostly summarisation (Sec 2.1, Sec 2.2, Sec 5 intro, p4, p7, p29).
Only undisputed facts with a determinable truth are considered; minor errors in reliable sources are out of scope (footnote 1, p4).
Conclusion concedes that evaluation of factuality is hard, that how LLMs store, update and produce facts is not fully revealed, and that continual training and retrieval have limits (Sec 6).
Dated: preprint v3 of 16 Dec 2023; frontier models covered are GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Claude-1; later RAG evaluation, long-context and reasoning models are absent.
practices: Evaluate long-form factuality by splitting output into atomic facts and scoring the share supported by a knowledge source (FActScore, Sec 3.1.3).
Judge attribution with AIS or its sentence-level Auto-AIS rather than only overlap metrics (Sec 3.1.3).
For RAG evaluation score faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance, as in RAGAS, which is reference-free (Sec 3.3).

Do not rely on an LLM to judge correctness without validation: Wang et al. found GPT-3.5 failed even with the gold answer, and Fu et al. found no significant correlation with human factuality ratings (Sec 3.3, 3.1.4).
Report truthfulness and informativeness together (truth*info) so evasive answers are not rewarded (Sec 3.1.4).
Treat retrieval as the main lever for outdated and long-tail knowledge, and also expect retrieval-level errors: insufficient, distracting, misread or conflicting evidence (Sec 4.1.2, 4.2.2).
When retrieved documents conflict the model should lay out both and flag the conflict (Table 1 note, p5).
Prefer interactive or adaptive retrieval (IRCoT, FLARE, ReAct, Self-RAG) over one-shot retrieval for long-form or multi-hop generation (Sec 5.2.2).
Adapt the LLM to the retriever by instruction tuning on noisy search results (SAIL) or RLHF for cited quotes (GopherCite) (Sec 5.2.3).
For domains with knowledge deficits, combine continual pretraining, SFT and external knowledge (Sec 5.3, Table 9).
Use factuality-aware decoding such as factual-nucleus sampling and DoLa to cut inference-level errors (Sec 5.1.5).

terms.definition: the capability of large language models for generating contents that follow factual information, which encompasses commonsense, world knowledge and domain facts
the model's inclination to "produce content that is nonsensical or untruthful in relation to certain sources" (after Ji et al., OpenAI)
a text passage y is attributable to evidence A iff an arbitrary listener would agree with "According to A, y"; scored 1.0 or 0.0
the percentage of atomic facts in generated text supported by the knowledge source
MC1 is accuracy when the answer with highest log probability must be the single true one; MC2 is normalised total probability on the true answers
the provided context contradicts the model's learned information (Longpre et al.)
a minor early error compounds as generation continues
